source_text: Aeque benedici per deos nationum Christo initiatus non sustinebit, ut non semper reiciat immundam benedictionem et eam sibi in deum conuertens emundet. benedici per deos nationum maledici est per deum. si cui dedero eleemosynam uel aliquid praestitero beneficii, et ille mihi deos suos uel coloniae genium propitios imprecetur, iam oblatio mea uel operatio idolorum honor erit, per quae benedictionis gratiam compensat. cur autem non sciat me dei causa fecisse, ut et deus potius glorificetur et daemonia non honorentur in eo quod propter deum feci ? si deus uidet, quoniam propter ipsum feci, pariter uidet, quoniam propter ipsum fecisse me nolui ostendere, et praeceptum eius idolothytum quodammodo feci. multi dicunt, nemo se debet promulgare; puto autem nec negare. negat enim, quicumque dissimulat in quacumque causa pro ethnico habitus, et utique omnis negatio idololatria est, sicut omnis idololatria negatio siue in factis siue in uerbis.
thought_title: Blessings by pagan gods are idolatry
orientation: Tertullian is warning believers that receiving a blessing in the name of pagan gods is a form of idolatry, even when it comes as thanks for a good deed.
pass_a_gloss: Equally [to be] blessed through [the] gods of [the] nations [one] initiated into Christ will not endure, so that [he] may not always reject [the] unclean blessing and, turning it for himself into God, cleanse [it]. [To be] blessed through [the] gods of [the] nations is [to be] cursed through God. If to anyone I shall have given alms or shall have furnished anything of kindness, and that [person] to me his gods or [the] genius of [the] colony [as] favorable shall invoke, now my offering or [my] work [will be] an honor of idols, through which [things] [he] repays [the] favor of [the] blessing. But why should [he] not know that I [have] done [it] for God's sake, so that both God rather may be glorified and demons may not be honored in that which for God's sake I did? If God sees that for his own sake I did [it], equally [he] sees that for his own sake I did not wish to show that I did [it], and his precept [I] made [into] a thing offered to idols in a certain way. Many say, no one ought to make himself known; but I think not even to deny. For [he] denies, whoever conceals in any cause [being] held as a pagan, and certainly every denial is idolatry, just as every idolatry [is] denial whether in deeds or in words.

choices.english: being blessed through the gods of the nations
choices.why: Keeps the passive force of benedici and the instrumental per, which is the point: the blessing comes through pagan gods.
Initiatus is a technical term for baptismal initiation; rendering it as 'initiated into Christ' preserves the ritual sense.
Genius is a specific Roman tutelary deity; keeping the Latin term with 'of the colony' preserves the local civic cult reference.
rejected: the guardian spirit of the colony

choices.why: The glossary gives 'things offered to idols' for idolothyta; using the singular form here matches the source's singular neuter.

choices.english: no one ought to make himself known
choices.why: Promulgare means to publish or make publicly known; 'make himself known' captures the reflexive sense of advertising one's faith.
rejected: no one ought to broadcast himself

choices.why: The glossary requires 'pagans' for ethnici; 'held as' preserves the passive sense of habitus.

pass_b_english: In the same way, someone initiated into Christ will not put up with being blessed through the gods of the pagans. He will not always reject the unclean blessing, but will turn it to God and cleanse it for himself. To be blessed through the gods of the pagans is to be cursed through God.

If I give someone alms or do him any kindness, and he then invokes his gods or the guardian spirit of his colony to be favorable to me, my gift or my work will become an honor to idols, because he repays the favor of the blessing through them. Why should he not know that I did it for God's sake, so that God rather may be glorified and demons not be honored in what I did for God? If God sees that I did it for His sake, He equally sees that I did not want to show that I did it for His sake, and I have in some way made His command into a thing offered to idols.

Many say that no one ought to make himself known; but I think he ought not even to deny it. For whoever conceals himself in any matter, being held as a pagan, denies—and certainly every denial is idolatry, just as every idolatry is denial, whether in deeds or in words.

problems.quote: He will always reject the unclean blessing
problems.source_quote: ut non semper reiciat immundam benedictionem
problems.why: Latin says “so that he does not always reject…”, English adds “always”, reversing the negation.
problems.fix: He will not always reject the unclean blessing, but will turn it to God.
problems.ruling: ut non semper reiciat = 'so that he does not always reject'; English 'will always reject' reverses the negation of non semper.

edits.old: He will always reject the unclean blessing and cleanse it for himself by turning it toward God.
edits.new: He will not always reject the unclean blessing, but will turn it to God and cleanse it for himself.

fixed: The English added 'always' and reversed the negation. The source says 'ut non semper reiciat' — 'so that he does not always reject' — meaning he does not always reject it, but turns it to God and cleanses it. Fixed to match.

problems.quote: but I think he ought not even to deny himself.
problems.why: Source says 'I think one ought not even to deny [faith]', not 'deny himself'. The verb is about denying one's faith, a key point.
problems.fix: but I think he ought not even to deny it.
problems.ruling: Latin lacks object; English adds 'himself', altering the sense of what is denied.

edits.old: but I think he ought not even to deny himself.
edits.new: but I think he ought not even to deny it.

fixed: Changed 'deny himself' to 'deny it' because the source 'puto autem nec negare' refers to denying one's faith, not denying oneself.

problems.why: Same concept (non-Christians) rendered as 'nations,' 'pagans,' and 'outsiders' interchangeably.
problems.fix: Use 'pagans' consistently or note that 'nations' = pagans.

edits.old: the gods of the nations is to be cursed
edits.new: the gods of the pagans is to be cursed

fixed: The source uses 'nationum' (of the nations), which the glossary maps to 'pagans' for non-Christians. Changed both occurrences of 'the gods of the nations' to 'the gods of the pagans' for consistency with the glossary.

last_rejected.quote: He will not always reject the unclean blessing, but will turn it to God and cleanse it for himself.
last_rejected.source_quote: ut non semper reiciat immundam benedictionem et eam sibi in deum conuertens emundet
last_rejected.why: Source says he WILL always reject it; English says he will NOT always reject it.
last_rejected.fix: so that he always rejects the unclean blessing and, turning it to God, cleanses it for himself.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'ut non semper reiciat' = 'that he may not always reject', matches English.

polish.changed: Standardized 'the nations' to 'the pagans' throughout, clarified 'the genius of the colony' as 'the guardian spirit of his colony,' and kept the argument's flow and all qualifications intact.

notes.why: Same concept (non-Christians) rendered as 'nations,' 'pagans,' and 'outsiders' interchangeably.
notes.fix: Use 'pagans' consistently or note that 'nations' = pagans.

notes.why: Roman tutelary spirit of a colony; unexplained concept.
notes.fix: Note: 'genius = tutelary spirit presiding over a place or person.'

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker's voice and pronoun references, kept the argument's turns in distinct paragraphs, and smoothed sentence rhythm for reading aloud without altering any claims or Scripture references.

notes.quote: Many say that no one ought to make himself known
